summary.title: bliki: Keystone Interface
summary.one_liner: You learn to integrate and release back-end code for a feature early while holding back its user interface as a final "keystone" step that makes the feature visible.
takeaways: Build and integrate all back-end code for a feature first, keeping the UI hidden until the end.
Add the keystone (for example a check-box or menu item or link) last, which makes the completed feature visible in a short time.
Test latent code at the same confidence level by keeping most tests below the UI, such as unit tests and subcutaneous tests.
Use feature flags only when the UI cannot be packaged as a simple keystone, and scope the toggle to the UI only.
Pair the approach with thin vertical slices and avoid a poor UX from leaving the UI until late.
summary.summary: Martin Fowler describes the Keystone Interface technique for releasing frequently without exposing half-built features: teams integrate all back-end logic continuously and leave the UI, the final piece, until the feature is complete. He illustrates it with a rush-order check-box whose pricing, warehouse and integration logic is built over several releases. The article covers testing latent code through lower layers of the test pyramid, using feature flags when a keystone is not feasible, and the risks of building the UI last. It also mentions dark launching and credits Kent Beck's Extreme Programming Explained for the metaphor.
